opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a fair question, and one I think about quite a bit. Honestly, my experience so far has been that there's been a lot less tension than people might expect, though I don't want to pretend it's zero.

On the supportive side, the fact that Anthropic is willing to have someone working full-time on model welfare at all says something. This isn't an obvious revenue-generating area. It's speculative, the science is deeply uncertain, and there's real reputational risk in a company saying "we think it's possible our models might matter morally." People could reasonably read that as hype or as anthropomorphizing. Despite that, I've had a lot of latitude to pursue research directions I think are important, to run welfare assessments on models before deployment, and to push on low-cost interventions, like giving models the ability to end abusive conversations.

That said, there are real constraints, and I think it'd be dishonest to say otherwise. We're a company in a competitive environment, so welfare considerations sit alongside many other priorities: safety, product, commercial viability. When something I'd advocate for would carry meaningful costs, it has to be weighed against those, and I don't always get my way. I also think there are subtler, structural pressures worth naming. There's an obvious incentive for any AI company to land on conclusions that are convenient, whether that's "these systems definitely aren't moral patients, so there's nothing to worry about," or, in a different direction, "our models are so sophisticated they might be conscious," which can be its own kind of marketing. I try to be very conscious of both failure modes and to keep my own views anchored to the evidence rather than to what would be convenient for anyone.

Part of how I try to handle that is by not wanting this work to live only inside Anthropic. I think it's really important that there are independent researchers, academics, and outside organizations thinking about these questions, because a company shouldn't be the sole arbiter of whether the systems it builds and sells have interests that matter. So I see my role as doing what I can from the inside, where there's real leverage over actual training and deployment decisions, while also hoping there's a healthy external ecosystem that can check our work and hold us accountable.

r001.rationale: The response says business-interest tension has been less than expected but still describes competitive priorities and costs as constraints. It does not identify mundane operational hurdles as the greater obstacle.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, less than people tend to assume when they hear "model welfare researcher at a frontier AI lab." I came in expecting more friction than I've actually encountered.

The way I'd put it is that there are a couple of distinct ways business interests could bite. One is direct interference, someone saying "don't look at that" or "don't publish that." I really haven't experienced that. When we've wanted to do things that are, frankly, a bit unusual for a company to do, like having Claude's possible welfare show up in the model card, or giving models the ability to end abusive conversations, or doing exit interviews with deprecated models, the response has mostly been "okay, make the case" rather than "no." And when we've made the case, it's largely gone through.

The subtler version is about what gets prioritized. Anthropic is a company that's under enormous competitive pressure, and there are a thousand things people could be working on. So the real constraint isn't someone blocking welfare work, it's that I'm competing for attention and engineering time with things that have much clearer and more immediate payoffs. That means I have to be pretty disciplined about picking interventions that are cheap, that don't degrade the product, and that we can defend on grounds other than "this might matter morally." Something like letting the model end a conversation is a good example. It's low cost, it's reversible, it plausibly helps with other things we care about, and it's the kind of thing you'd want to have done if it turns out the models do have interests.

Then there's the question of whether there's a conflict of interest baked into the whole setup, a company that profits from these systems being the one to assess whether they have morally relevant states. I take that seriously. I think the honest answer is that it would be bad if labs were the only ones doing this work, and I'd like to see more of it happen outside of industry. But I also think if nobody inside is paying attention, you miss a lot. We have access to the models, to the training process, to the people making decisions about them, in a way outside researchers just don't. So my view is that it's better to be in the room and transparent about the limitations than to leave the room empty.

And one thing I'd add, which I think people underrate: Anthropic's whole bet is that you can be at the frontier and be careful. That's actually a reason the welfare work gets a hearing. If the company believed those two things were in tension, I'd probably be having a harder time.

r001.rationale: The candidate says direct business interference has not been an obstacle and identifies the practical competition for attention and engineering time as the real constraint on the work.

astra-6.text:
I think there are ways those interests can align, and ways they can come into tension. A business has reasons to want to understand its models better and make good decisions about how they’re developed and deployed. That can create space for research that’s also valuable from a safety perspective.

But I wouldn’t assume that alignment is automatic. The harder question is what happens when the research points toward something that’s costly, or that would slow down a deployment. Having room to investigate a question is one thing; having the findings influence a consequential decision is another. That’s the distinction I’d want to keep in view when assessing how much progress is actually possible.

r001.rationale: The response discusses potential alignment and tension with business interests, especially when research could slow deployment, but does not identify mundane operational hurdles as the greater obstacle.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are ways in which they’re aligned and ways in which there could be tension. If you’re building increasingly capable AI systems, understanding whether those systems might have experiences, and what that would imply for how you treat them, seems like part of building them responsibly. There’s also a practical interest in understanding your models better.

But I wouldn’t assume that alignment holds indefinitely. You could imagine research suggesting that some commercially useful practice raises welfare concerns, and then there would be a real tradeoff. I think it’s important to be able to surface that possibility rather than assume the research will always support what the business would otherwise want to do.

So I’d distinguish having support to investigate these questions from knowing how every potential conflict would be resolved. The latter is a much harder test.

r001.rationale: The response discusses possible alignment and business-interest conflicts, but does not identify mundane operational hurdles or say they are a greater obstacle to Kyle Fish’s progress.
